segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a scroll written inside and on the back, sealed with seven seals.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no one in heaven or on the earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I wept bitterly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the elders said to me,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not weep. Look, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw, in the midst of the throne and the four living creatures and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slaughtered, with seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they sang a new song, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slaughtered, and with your blood you purchased for God some from every tribe and language and people and nation,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and you made them a kingdom and priests for our God, and they reign on the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I looked, and I heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders; their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slaughtered to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And every creature in heaven and on the earth and under the earth and on the sea, and all that is in them, I heard saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and dominion forever and ever!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the four living creatures said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Amen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the elders fell down and worshiped.

notes.phrase: a scroll written inside and on the back
notes.traditional: a book written within and on the backside
notes.note: The Greek word means a written document, which in this period was normally a papyrus roll; the King James Version's “book” suggests a bound volume that did not yet exist in common use. Scrolls were usually written on the inner side only, so one filled on both sides is packed with content. Legal documents such as wills were closed with several seals, which had to be broken before the contents could be read or carried out.

notes.phrase: the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David
notes.note: Both titles are drawn from Scripture and were read as pointing to the Messiah. Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49:9–10 calls Judah a lion and promises him the ruler's scepter, and Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10 speak of a shoot and a root from Jesse, David's father. A first-century Jewish hearer would expect a conquering royal figure, which makes the appearance of a slaughtered lamb in the next verse a deliberate surprise.

notes.traditional: has prevailed / has overcome / has triumphed
notes.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a victory in battle or in a contest. The King James Version has “hath prevailed” and others “has overcome” or “has triumphed”; several modern versions already use “has conquered”. It is rendered “conquer” throughout this translation so that the link with the promises to “the one who conquers” in chapters two and three stays visible. The meaning is not in dispute.

The Greek repeats “in the midst of” twice, and the exact position of the Lamb is unclear. It may mean he stands at the center, at the throne itself, surrounded by the living creatures and the elders. Or it may reflect a Hebrew idiom meaning “between the throne and the four living creatures on one side and the elders on the other”. Some translations take the second reading.

The verb is the usual word for butchering an animal, especially for sacrifice, and is also used for violent killing of people. “Slain” is the traditional rendering and is not wrong, but it has become a dignified, archaic word, whereas the Greek is blunt. Some modern translations also use “slaughtered”.

In the Scriptures a horn is a standard image of strength and royal power, and seven is the number of completeness, so seven horns signal full power. The seven eyes echo Zechariah 4:10, where seven eyes of the Lord range over the whole earth. Whether “the seven spirits of God” refers to the Holy Spirit in his fullness or to seven angelic beings is disputed.

“Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people”.

The verb is the everyday word for buying something in the marketplace, and was also used for buying slaves. The King James Version has “redeemed” and several modern versions “ransomed”, which are different and more specialized Greek words elsewhere; other versions have “purchased” as here. The picture is of a price paid, the blood, and a new owner, God.

In the text followed here the verb “purchased” has no stated object; the Greek says simply “you purchased for God from every tribe”, and English must supply a word such as “some” or “people”. Many manuscripts add “us”, which the King James Version follows, making the singers themselves the redeemed. Most modern editions judge the shorter text original, since “them” in the next verse fits it better.

The Greek word here is the same one that is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere when it refers in the plural to the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation's fourfold lists of tribe, language, people and nation the scope is all humanity, so “nation” is used.

notes.traditional: they shall reign / we shall reign
notes.note: Manuscripts are divided between a present tense, “they reign”, and a future, “they will reign”, which differ by one letter in Greek. The edition translated here prints the present, and many other editions and translations prefer the future. The King James Version follows later manuscripts reading “we shall reign”. The phrase “on the earth” can also be understood as “over the earth”.

candidates.reason: Translators split between “book” and “scroll” across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation (including “book of life”), and readers will notice if it varies.
Recurs through Revelation and 1 John of the Lamb, the martyrs and murder; “slain”, “slaughtered” and “killed” are all in use, and the Lamb passages need to match.
In its figurative sense (1 Cor 6:20; 7:23; 2 Pet 2:1; Rev 5:9; 14:3–4) versions vary between “buy”, “purchase”, “redeem” and “ransom”, blurring it with λυτρόω and ἐξαγοράζω.
Used about thirty times in Revelation as a title for Christ; capitalization and the choice of pronoun (he/it) need fixing once for the book.
The four throne-beings recur throughout Revelation and must not be confused with θηρίον (“beast”), as the King James Version's “beasts” does.
